title: Contract labour: the largest hidden workforce
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Around two in five factory workers are hired through contractors. The ASI data, the OSH Code rules on licensing and core activities, and BMS's demands.
body:
Walk through any large factory, port, mine, hospital or office complex and you will find people doing the same kind of work in the same place, wearing similar uniforms, but employed on very different terms. Some are on the rolls of the company. Others are on the rolls of a contractor. The second group is the "contract workforce", and it has become one of the largest and least visible parts of Indian industry.

## How big is it?

The best official count comes from the Annual Survey of Industries, which covers registered factories. Reports on its results for 2022-23 say that about **5.95 million of 14.61 million workers**, or **40.7 percent**, in about 253,000 factories were employed through contractors, the highest share recorded up to that point. The share was 38.4 percent in 2019-20, before the pandemic, and 40.2 percent in 2021-22. A later report on the 2023-24 survey puts the share at about **42 percent**, the highest since 1997-98, against about 20 percent in 1999-2000.

The figures vary sharply by State. In 2022-23, the contract share was highest in Bihar (68.6 percent), Telangana (64.5 percent), Uttarakhand (57.7 percent), Odisha (57.3 percent) and Maharashtra (53 percent), and lowest in Kerala (23.8 percent), Tamil Nadu (24.5 percent) and Punjab (29.8 percent). These numbers cover only factories. They do not count contract workers in construction, services, security, housekeeping, public sector undertakings or government offices, where the share may be larger still.

## Why it matters

Contract workers often do the same work as permanent employees but are paid less, hold no security of tenure, and may have no leave, bonus or social security. A contractor can be replaced at the end of a work order, and the workers can be replaced with him. A worker engaged for ten years through three successive contractors may have no service record at all. Unions therefore see contracting not only as a wage issue but as a question of dignity and bargaining power: it is difficult to negotiate collectively when the person who signs the pay cheque is not the person who controls the work.

## The legal framework

The **Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970** was the central law on the subject. It required licensing of contractors, regulated wages and welfare facilities, and allowed the Government to prohibit contract labour in certain circumstances. It applied to establishments with twenty or more contract workers.

Since the Labour Codes were brought into effect on 21 November 2025, these provisions form part of the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Code, 2020**. An explainer on the Code summarises the key points:

- **Threshold.** The contract labour chapter applies to establishments that employ fifty or more contract workers (the figure was twenty under the 1970 Act), and to contractors supplying that many workers. Intermittent or casual work is excluded: work done for more than 120 days in a year is not treated as intermittent.
- **Licensing.** A covered contractor needs a licence. A regular licence is valid for five years, and the contractor may not recover the licensing costs from workers. A common licence for operations across States is available through a central authority.
- **Core activities.** Contract labour is generally barred from an establishment's **core activities**, meaning those it was set up to perform and those essential or necessary to them. Sanitation, security, canteen, loading and unloading, transport, housekeeping and some construction and maintenance work are listed as not core, and there are exceptions where the work is ordinarily outsourced, does not need full-time workers, or arises from a sudden surge in work. The wording of these exceptions will decide how much of the restriction survives in practice.
- **Principal employer's liability.** The principal employer must provide the specified welfare facilities directly, and the contractor is primarily responsible for wages. If the contractor fails to pay or short-pays, the principal employer must pay the balance and may recover it from the contractor. Engaging an unlicensed contractor is itself a contravention, and an indemnity clause in the contract does not cure it.
- **Experience certificate.** A contractor must give a worker an experience certificate on request.

The Labour Ministry's summary of the Codes adds that principal employers are to provide health and social security benefits to contract workers and free annual health check-ups, and that fixed-term employees get the same benefits as permanent staff, with gratuity after one year of service instead of five.

## What the Code leaves for debate

Thresholds and exceptions are where unions and employers disagree. Raising the threshold from twenty to fifty means that a smaller number of establishments fall under the licensing regime. The core-activity prohibition, on the other hand, is a rule that many unions have sought for decades, but exceptions for work that "does not require full-time workers" or arises from a "sudden surge" are broad terms and can be stretched. Which side of the line a particular job falls on will depend on how the Government's rules define these terms and how inspectors apply them.

## BMS's position

BMS has a federation for this sector, the **Akhil Bharatiya Theka Mazdoor Mahasangh**, among the thirty-eight federations listed on its website. Its demands have been consistent. At its national conference in Puri in February 2026, BMS adopted a resolution on contract workers that calls the system discriminatory when it is used for cost-cutting, including for permanent and perennial work, and that asks for **equal pay for equal work**, social security coverage, protection against arbitrary termination, strict enforcement against misuse of the contract system and accountability of principal employers. It said workers in core activities "should not be treated as disposable manpower."

In an earlier nationwide protest call, in 2018, BMS also asked for an immediate meeting of the Central Advisory Contract Labour Board, the formation of State advisory boards as the law provides, regularisation of contract labour as the Act provides, an increase in the liability of principal employers and amendment of the 1970 Act. The point it has made repeatedly is that the law itself speaks of abolishing contract labour where possible and of decent conditions otherwise, and that neither has been fully implemented.

## What a contract worker should do

1. **Ask for a written appointment letter** and a wage slip. The Labour Codes make appointment letters mandatory for all workers.
2. **Check that PF and ESI contributions are being deposited**, using the member portals, and keep your UAN safe.
3. **Keep your own record** of attendance, wages paid, the name of the contractor and the principal employer, and the work you do.
4. **Know who the principal employer is.** If wages are not paid, a complaint can be directed to the principal employer as well as the contractor.
5. **Join a union.** A single worker rarely wins an argument with a contractor. A union can raise the matter with the principal employer, the labour department and the licensing authority.

## What employers can do

Verify that the contractor holds a valid licence, review wage registers regularly, pay the contractor on time so that he can pay the worker, and ask whether the work really needs to be contracted at all. A workplace in which the same task is done on two different wage scales will not be a settled one.

## Closing

Contracting is legal. Exploitation is not. Whether the Labour Codes reduce the second without destroying the first will depend less on the text of the law than on its rules, its inspectors and the willingness of principal employers to accept that the people who work in their premises are their responsibility.
